cards.back: A bar graph that shows the frequency of data values in intervals of the same size. It reveals the shape of a data distribution.
The right side of the histogram is approximately a mirror image of the left side. The mean and median are about equal.
The tail of the histogram extends to the left. Most of the data are on the right. The mean is usually less than the median.
The tail of the histogram extends to the right. Most of the data are on the left. The mean is usually greater than the median.
All the bars of the histogram are about the same height. It is a type of symmetric distribution.

cards.front: For a symmetric distribution, which measures of center and spread should you use?
cards.back: Use the [[imp:mean]] to describe the center and the [[imp:standard deviation]] to describe the spread.

cards.front: For a skewed distribution, which measures of center and spread should you use?
cards.back: Use the [[imp:median]] to describe the center and the [[imp:five-number summary]] to describe the spread.

cards.front: Why is the median preferred over the mean for skewed data?
cards.back: The median is resistant to extreme values. The mean gets pulled toward the tail, making it less representative of the typical value.
Two histograms placed back‑to‑back or side‑by‑side on the same axes. Used to compare the distributions of two data sets.

cards.front: State the [[kw:Empirical Rule]] for bell‑shaped distributions.
cards.back: About 68% of data lie within 1 SD of the mean. About 95% lie within 2 SDs. About 99.7% lie within 3 SDs. Only applies to bell‑shaped, symmetric data.

cards.front: Male heights are bell‑shaped with mean 70 in and SD 3 in. What percent of men are between 67 and 73 inches tall?
cards.back: 67 to 73 is mean ± 1 SD. By the Empirical Rule, about [[imp:68%]] of men fall in this range.

cards.front: Women own a mean of 14 pairs of shoes with SD 4, bell‑shaped. About how many of 40 women own between 10 and 18 pairs?
cards.back: 10 to 18 is mean ± 1 SD → about 68%. 0.68 × 40 ≈ [[imp:27]] women.

cards.front: When is a data value considered unusual in a bell‑shaped distribution?
cards.back: When it lies more than [[imp:2 standard deviations]] from the mean. About 95% of data lie within 2 SDs.

cards.front: How can you tell if a distribution is skewed left from a box‑and‑whisker plot?
cards.back: The left whisker is longer than the right whisker. Most data are on the right side of the plot.

cards.front: How can you tell if a distribution is skewed right from a histogram?
cards.back: The tail of the histogram extends to the right. Most of the data are on the left.
